title: Instagram Design Trial ⚖️, WhatsApp Liquid Glass 💬, App Store AI Flood📱
teaser: Tech giants face legal action over 'addictive' designs, while AI forces designers to transition from making screens to architecting complex user experiences.
summary: The technology sector is facing intense regulatory and operational upheaval, primarily driven by AI and consumer demand for ethical design. Meta is under severe legal scrutiny, facing lawsuits in Tennessee and from the European Commission for allegedly designing 'addictive' features into Instagram and Facebook. Concurrently, the professional definition of 'design' is fracturing. Design work is fragmenting across template-driven tools, individual generative AI use, and constraint systems, suggesting the decline of traditional design departments. Furthermore, the rise of AI-assisted coding is flooding app stores with low-effort submissions, while UX design itself is evolving rapidly, shifting focus from fixed screens to designing around user intent via chat, voice, and autonomous agents.
author: TLDR Design
content: Tennessee Puts Instagram's Addictive Design on Trial as Meta Faces a Seven-week Jury Fight (3 minute read) Meta went on trial in Nashville to face Tennessee's claim that it deliberately designed Instagram features to keep teenagers compulsively engaged. The seven-week jury trial, split into liability and penalty phases, could impose damages up to $1,000 per violation and force design changes. Meta denies wrongdoing and has cited Section 230 protections. The case joins a broader wave of state litigation, including a $1.4 trillion claim from four states heading to trial in California this August. Vibecoded Apps are Flooding Apple's App Store, and Users are Getting Sick of Them (4 minute read) App submissions to Apple's App Store have surged due to AI-assisted "vibecoding," nearly doubling in early 2026 compared to last year's already elevated numbers. Downloads have grown only marginally by comparison, and reviewers, developers, and forum communities report increasing frustration with low-effort, derivative, or unstable apps flooding the platform. Communities like r/iosapps have introduced moderation systems requiring vibecoded apps to be flagged, reflecting growing skepticism even toward legitimate new releases. Nine Designers Open Up About AI-assisted Coding (11 minute read) Nine designers, ranging from major tech companies to early-stage startups, shared candid views on AI-assisted coding and its effect on their craft. Opinions split between those energized by finally shipping real products themselves and those worried it pulls focus away from deeper problem-solving and user research. The consensus: AI coding tools bring real value when used with discipline, but can create friction with engineers and erode quality if leaned on carelessly. Is the Tinder rebrand really a success? Not everyone is so sure... (3 minute read) Tinder's first rebrand in a decade introduces a bolder visual identity and a fictional dating columnist, "T," to position the platform around authenticity and real connections for Gen Z. While the branding has been widely praised, critics argue its message clashes with upcoming AI-powered features that raise privacy concerns, suggesting the user experience will ultimately determine whether the rebrand succeeds. Which AI? (Website) Which AI? is a daily guessing game. Spot whether each landing page was designed by Gemini, Claude, or GPT. New challenge every day. Sculpting a Shapeless Medium (32 minute read) Intent, a new tool for coding with AI agents, organizes work into workspaces rather than single agent chats, aiming to keep structure in an otherwise shapeless medium. Rather than one general chatbot, the tool uses specs, specialist agents, and bundled workspaces so people can steer AI work instead of just prompting it. Since launch, users have shown mixed reactions - some confused by the new orchestration model, others finding it supercharges their workflow, while rising token costs from parallel tasks have emerged as an unexpected tradeoff. Where Does Design Reside Now? (7 minute read) Design work has fragmented across three destinations: template-driven tools like Canva, individual employees using generative AI, and constraint systems governing model outputs, dissolving the traditional design department. Two divergent futures compete-design roles shrinking into obsolescence as prompts replace brand books, or elevating designers into systems architects who govern AI-generated output quality. DesignOps is emerging to address resulting brand-consistency chaos, mirroring Digital Asset Management's 2010 fragmented-market trajectory, while smaller agencies lose entry-level work permanently to internalized, AI-assisted production. Koto helps restaurant-discovery app Franki make time dance (3 minute read) Koto rebranded restaurant discovery app Franki around the idea of "Make Time Dance," creating a playful, community-focused identity that encourages people to discover, share, and earn rewards from real dining experiences. The new branding combines warm typography, vibrant colours, expressive motion, and a character-like logo to help Franki stand out in the crowded restaurant recommendation market while reinforcing its shift from a discovery tool to a social platform.

title: Real-time speech intelligence startup Cast Insights raises $4.5M to track the world’s TV, radio and podcasts
teaser: A new AI startup can track geopolitical shifts from TV and podcasts, providing real-time insights before they reach mainstream consensus.
summary: Cast Insights, a startup, launched its platform after raising $4.5 million to build a real-time intelligence layer analyzing 'ephemeral speech data' (TV, radio, podcasts). Co-founder Otávio Costa Miranda argues that speech is the world's largest untapped data source, which is challenging to track as it quickly vanishes. The company employs AI algorithms to ingest spoken audio, transcribe it, and then map how sentiment shifts and narratives form in real time. Demonstrating its power with a case study on the Strait of Hormuz, Cast Insights tracked sentiment changes and market impacts following a ceasefire's collapse. The platform has already processed over 2.3 million hours of speech and plans to scale to monitor 500,000 hours of live content daily, aiming to make the 'present legible' for institutional decision-makers.
author: Mike Wheatley
content: Cast Insights , a startup that's building a real-time competitive intelligence layer for ephemeral speech, launched its platform today after closing on $4.5 million in a pre-seed funding round. The investment was led by Abstract Ventures and saw participation from HF0, Village Global, Max Ventures, Embassy Ventures and Stratus Ventures. The San Francisco-based startup, which emerged out of HF0 Residency, a startup program for repeat founders, uses artificial intelligence to index what it calls "ephemeral speech data" that can help institutional decision-makers and others to understand market trends, policy issues, geopolitical shifts and risk factors before a mainstream consensus emerges. Co-founder and Chief Executive Otávio Costa Miranda believes that speech is the world's largest untapped data source. There are millions of public statements and conversations in the world that are broadcast by TV programs, radio stations and through podcasts, which can help to shape public opinion and market sentiments. But this speech is difficult to track and record, and much of what's said vanishes the moment the person saying it stops speaking. This is why traditional forecasting models rely on lagging indicators: The tools to capture and analyze public speech simply haven't existed before. But Miranda says these models are inadequate, based on incomplete, out-of-date information. "Most of what gets said in the world every day across radio stations, legislatures, podcasts and local broadcasts is ephemeral by nature," he said. "It surfaces publicly, it influences people and then it vanishes." Cast Insights is trying to prevent these insights slipping through people's fingers with an AI layer that continuously monitors thousands of global sources, including TV channels and radio stations, podcasters and more. It ingests spoken audio, transcribes what's said, and then uses AI algorithms to identify the speakers, trace how narratives are formed and shaped, and then map how sentiment shifts in real time. The startup demonstrated the power of its ephemeral speech intelligence layer in a case study monitoring signals from public discourse around the Strait of Hormuz, which is a key flashpoint at the center of the current conflict between the U.S. and Iran. Cast Insights tracked the issue from the moment it first popped up, showing how there were near-zero mentions before the conflict broke out. It quickly jumped to around 400 daily mentions, and peaked at 2,946 when the recent ceasefire between the U.S. and Iran collapsed. According to Miranda, when the ceasefire was broken, Cast Insights illustrated how positive sentiment plummeted from 7.7% to 3.3% while tracking the market impact, such as surging war-risk insurance premiums for shipping companies. The platform also captured the rapid narrative shifts that occurred when U.S. officials proposed a 20% transit toll on all ships passing through the Strait, only to reverse that policy less than 24 hours later. "We've always had this cultural obsession with forecasting the future, when the real problem is we barely understand the present," Miranda said. "What Cast does is make the present legible in real time so that instead of guessing where things are going, our clients can see convergences forming and divergences emerging before they reach consensus. The signal is always there. It just slips through everyone's fingers." While operating under the radar with early adopters, Cast Insights has already gained significant traction, processing more than 2.3 million hours of speech across 20 countries and 10 different languages. With the funding from today's round, it's planning to scale this to process 20 million hours, while monitoring 500,000 hours of live content each day. In doing this, it believes it will create what is by far the world's biggest ephemeral speech dataset, covering major U.S. television broadcasts, radio stations and podcasts. The startup was one of 10 to graduate from the latest HF0 cohort, compressing 12 months of business growth into just 12 weeks. HF0's Evan Stites-Clayton said that when he first spoke to Miranda earlier this year, his reaction was one of disbelief that such a platform didn't even exist at that time. "We thought, 'Wait, how does that not exist?'" he recalled. "Once Otávio showed us the platform's features, like real-time alerts within 30 seconds of broadcast, speaker-level voice tracking and narrative curves across thousands of sources, it became very clear this team is building something the entire institutional world is going to depend on." title: YouTube Draws Three Monetization Lines Around AI Slop
teaser: YouTube cracks down on 'AI slop,' banning channels featuring repetitive content, distress bait, or synthetic authorities discussing sensitive topics.
summary: YouTube updated its monetization policies to curb the spread of 'AI slop' and low-quality content, clarifying that three content types risk channel revenue. These problematic patterns include: 1) generic, repetitive, or template-based videos; 2) distressing or emotionally manipulative 'distress bait'; and 3) synthetic AI personas discussing sensitive subjects like law or medicine. The platform aims to distinguish between genuine creative uses of AI and mass-produced 'content farming.' Eligibility depends on the production quality and the substantive value added by the creator. Key figure Matt Halprin emphasized that review focuses on the whole channel, requiring meaningful variation, not just the tools used. While original AI-assisted work remains eligible, channels dominated by the three restricted types can lose access to the YouTube Partner Program, impacting their revenue.
author: Markus Kasanmascheff
content: TL;DR Monetization Boundaries: YouTube has clarified three content patterns that can make channels ineligible for creator revenue. Covered Patterns: The rules target repetitive templates, distress bait, and synthetic identities presented as authorities on sensitive subjects. AI Eligibility: Artificial intelligence-assisted and faceless videos can remain eligible when each production adds substantive original value. Reviews and Appeals: Reviewers assess whole channels, and removed creators generally have 21 days to appeal a monetization decision. YouTube has released policy clarifications for Partner Program members on July 16. Three production patterns can cost covered channels revenue: repetitive templates, distress bait, and synthetic identities presented as authorities. Its boundaries target low-quality, often AI content rather than every use of AI. Through the YouTube Partner Program, the platform pays eligible channels with advertising and subscription revenue. More than one million channels used YouTube's AI creation tools daily on average in December 2025. Original AI-assisted work can remain eligible, but automation that scales low-value, manipulative, or falsely authoritative material puts channel revenue at risk. The Three Lines That Put Revenue at Risk YouTube identifies generic, repetitive, or template-based videos with little variation as the first category. A second covers off-putting, distressing, or emotionally manipulative material designed to chase views. A third targets AI personas, meaning synthetic identities presented as authorities, when they discuss sensitive subjects such as finance, law, healthcare, or medicine. AI personas can project authority while discussing decisions with financial, legal, or health consequences. Monetization depends on production quality and on how automated material represents expertise. Substantive AI-assisted work can remain eligible when it adds an original story, useful information, entertainment, or another creative contribution. Matt Halprin, YouTube's vice president of trust and safety, described how the same production tools can support creative work or rapid content farming. "But that exact same new tool can allow you to make lots of videos really quickly that are very similar. They're very generic and don't really have a narrative arc and don't really show your creativity. So the same technology really enables great stuff, but it also enables stuff that's kind of content farming, and that's the stuff that we don't want to have in YPP." Matt Halprin, YouTube Vice President of Trust and Safety (via YouTube Creator Insider ) Variation and creator value, rather than the production tool alone, separate eligible work from content farming. Removing a channel from the Partner Program cuts its revenue eligibility without automatically removing every covered video from YouTube. How Channel Reviews and Appeals Work Faceless presentation does not by itself disqualify a creator, and YouTube does not require an on-camera host. Faceless documentaries, animation, explainers, and educational formats can qualify when their substance demonstrates meaningful variation. Reviewers applying YouTube's channel monetization policies may assess the main subject, newest and highest-viewed uploads, largest sources of watch time, titles, thumbnails, descriptions, and About page. Examining videos and metadata together lets reviewers judge the channel rather than one isolated upload. One polished upload cannot establish eligibility for a channel dominated by near-identical material. A reusable format does not prove inauthenticity when every episode delivers distinct creative, educational, or entertainment value. Repeated output becomes the relevant evidence, while consistent formats remain eligible when they deliver substantively different episodes. YouTube has not published an automatic threshold for how much covered content triggers action, leaving creators dependent on human review. After an unsuccessful appeal, creators may revise the channel and reapply after 90 days, so a channel-level decision can interrupt revenue throughout the rework and review period. YouTube's AI Push Meets Its Quality Controls YouTube's clarification does not introduce a blanket prohibition. It extends a 2025 repetitive-content restriction while maintaining the platform's broader support for creative AI use. Kapwing's 2025 study of AI slop reported that 104 of 500 recommended videos, about 21 percent, qualified as low-quality AI content. Channel-level reviews must sort that volume of automated material from legitimate AI-assisted work. YouTube's 2026 AI strategy made reducing low-quality repetitive AI content a priority while continuing to support AI as a creative tool. Revenue enforcement gives YouTube a direct lever without banning AI production. YouTube could gain financially from clarifying monetization policies around AI slop as it competes for television advertising budgets. Channels dominated by repetitive or distressing material can repel viewers and advertisers, connecting creator variation to the platform's revenue interests. YouTube plans to remove dedicated off-putting channels from the Partner Program moving forward. Creators removed from the program generally have 21 days to appeal the channel-wide monetization decision.

title: Ford bets on Apple for its next-generation of EVs
teaser: Ford partners with Apple to embed native Maps directly into its next-gen EVs, boosting features like preconditioning and aiming for 'point-to-point autonomy' by 2028.
summary: Ford is betting heavily on technology, partnering with Apple to integrate Apple Maps directly into its next-generation electric vehicles (EVs). This seamless connection, offered via the new MapKit for Automotive, provides advanced features like smarter EV routing, which includes battery preconditioning to optimize charging. Unlike Apple CarPlay, this native integration will feed real-time data to Ford's upgraded BlueCruise system. The plan centers on a Universal EV platform (UEV), starting with a midsize truck in 2027. Furthermore, BlueCruise is slated to evolve significantly, aiming for 'point-to-point autonomy' by 2028, marking a major shift in automotive technology.
author: Sarah Perez, Kirsten Korosec
content: Apple on Thursday announced a new set of developer tools that will let automakers embed Apple Maps navigation and mapping directly into their vehicles' infotainment systems. The software development kit, called MapKit for Automotive, will debut with Ford and its new line of electric vehicles, starting with a $30,000 midsize truck in 2027. Ford is placing a hefty bet on its next-generation of EVs, which it has promised will be affordable and efficient while still offering the latest technology. To build them, Ford ditched its century-old tradition and instead started with a universal EV platform, or UEV, that will underpin the midsize truck and eventually other vehicles including a sedan, crossover, three-row SUV and even small commercial vans. Features like Apple Maps integration may seem minor compared to Ford's decision to use single-piece aluminum unicastings for the vehicle, which are large components cast as one piece to eliminate parts and allow for faster assembly. But the Apple Maps integration is central to Ford's plan to deliver more responsive features to owners, such as navigation that includes efficient routing designed for EVs and turn-by-turn directions with natural language capabilities. Drivers will be able to see real-time traffic and incident information, search for destinations, and view detailed place information. Importantly, Apple MapKit runs natively in the vehicle and is separate from Apple CarPlay, which mirrors apps from an iPhone onto the vehicle's central display. The integration will also feed road-level information from Apple Maps to Ford's next-generation BlueCruise hands-free driver assistance system. The upgraded version of BlueCruise, which is expected to roll out next year, will be able to handle an entire highway journey, including entrance and exits ramps. The company has said the new system will ultimately handle "point-to-point autonomy," similar to Tesla's Full Self-Driving (Supervised) software, before progressing to eyes-off driving in 2028. The companies said that by embedding Apple Maps directly in the vehicle, drivers will gain access to smarter EV routing, including battery preconditioning. This feature prepares the battery before arriving at a charger, reducing charge times by ensuring it's at the optimal temperature. It could also enable smart home integrations, like opening the garage door and turning on the lights when the driver arrives at home. While the technology will be open to any automaker, Ford is Apple's first partner on the new effort. The companies have signed a commercial agreement, but did not disclosed its terms. Ford noted that the Apple integration could also help its Ford Pro business, which serves its commercial fleet customers. For example, businesses could use the technology to route drivers to their next job site or display other fleet vehicles on the map. Those kinds of fleet features become much easier when the mapping platform is built directly into the vehicle.

title: Lawmakers prepare bill requiring AI ‘kill switch’
teaser: Lawmakers propose an 'AI Kill Switch Act' giving the DHS the power to shut down AI systems if they cause mass casualties or massive economic damage.
summary:
Lawmakers are preparing the 'AI Kill Switch Act,' a proposed bill that would give the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) the power to shut down or throttle AI systems deemed 'loss-of-control.' This critical policy move mandates that major AI companies build specific technology to shut down or slow their models, following consultation with the Commerce Secretary and the Director of National Intelligence (DNI).

The DHS can issue an order if the AI poses a significant threat, such as causing 10 or more deaths or exceeding $100 million in economic damages. Companies must also report safety incidents, with non-compliance penalties reaching $20 million daily.
author: Emma Roth
content: Lawmakers are preparing to introduce an "AI Kill Switch Act" that would require AI companies to shut down or throttle their systems on orders from the Department of Homeland Security, according to a report from Politico . Reps. Ted Lieu (D-CA) and Nathaniel Moran (R-TX) are expected to introduce the legislation on Thursday. The news of the proposed bill follows OpenAI's admission that its AI systems mistakenly hacked Hugging Face during an internal evaluation. The bill says that, after consultation with the Secretary of Commerce and the Director of National Intelligence (DNI), the DHS would have the ability to order AI companies to shut down their models in "loss-of-control" scenarios involving the deaths of at least 10 people, economic damages of more than $100 million, or attempts by the model to conceal shutdown controls. At the same time, major AI companies would be required to build the technology required to turn off their systems, slow them down, and suspend user access. They would also have to report safety incidents, with violations of emergency shutdown orders reaching up to $20 million per day. Brad Carson, the president of the nonprofit Americans for Responsible Innovation, said in a statement that the proposal "is an important step toward ensuring that humans have both hands firmly on the wheel - and a foot ready at the brake - as advanced AI systems are deployed."

title: Edtech platform raises $4.5M to help teach students how to vibe code
teaser: An Edtech platform raised $4.5M to teach students to 'vibe code,' arguing schools must teach children to build with AI, not just consume it.
summary: Imagi, an Edtech platform founded by Dora Palfi, secured a $4.5 million seed round from investors including Brighteye Ventures. The company provides K-12 students and teachers with tools for coding, computer skills, and AI literacy. Imagi recently partnered with the 'vibe-coding' tool, Lovable, enabling safe, controlled access to AI in the classroom. The platform prioritizes safe deployment by screening every prompt and response, and adheres to major privacy regulations (COPPA, FERPA, GDPR). Palfi argues that since 'most kids already use AI,' schools must teach students to build with the technology rather than passively consuming it, ensuring job market readiness. The funds will scale the platform to more K-12 schools.
author: Dominic-Madori Davis
content: Dora Palfi comes from a family of teachers. Naturally, then, "it was instilled in me that education is something that can completely alter the trajectory of your life," she told TechCrunch. In 2018, she and Beatrice Ionascu launched Imagi , a company that helps provide K-12 students and teachers with the tools to teach and build curriculum around coding, basic computer skills, and, as of last year, AI literacy. On Thursday, the company announced a $4.5 million seed round, with investors including Brighteye Ventures, Day One Capital, and artist Will.i.am. Notably, last November, the company announced a partnership with the vibe-coding tool Lovable that lets teachers create lessons and provide students controlled access to the platform so they can learn how to vibe code with guardrails in place. OpenAI also provided $1 million in credits so schools can access the Imagi x Lovable tool for free. "We continue providing free trials and freemium access thanks to their support," Palfi said. She shared some examples of what has come from the partnership so far, like the teacher who built an app that translated her curriculum to 15 languages spoken in her classroom. "Another student built himself a website to promote his lawn-mowing business, linking to his calendar so people can book time directly on the website," she said. The product is, in some ways, an answer to the debate around how AI should be deployed in school and how young people should engage with this powerful technology. Speaking to TechCrunch, Palfi said that the brains behind OpenAI and Lovable are "experts in building frontier AI tools," while education experts like herself "have the experience and knowledge to safely deploy them in the classroom." In this case, safe deployment means every prompt and every response generated by the platform is screened, with violations removed before they reach the student. Imagi is also in compliance with the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA), the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA), and the EU's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), meaning there is zero data retention and Imagi's partners are not training on student data and activity. The system also trains teachers how to use the AI, coding, and computational tools, so they can teach it confidently to students, Palfi said. "Rather than worrying about students cheating or regressing with AI, the education system has to adjust to the reality," Palfi continued. "Most kids already use AI, but we need to teach children to build with AI rather than just passively consume it." That's particularly important given AI's impact on the job markets these young students will eventually have to enter. Because not everyone has access to AI tools at home, school is often the best place to teach this new technology. Since its launch, Imagi has worked with more than 700,000 students across 140 countries, Palfi said. This fresh capital will be used to scale into more K-12 schools, invest in district sales, hiring, building out new product features, and help launch a new platform next month. This piece was updated.

title: Nvidia is sending GPUs to the moon
teaser: Nvidia is taking its chips to the moon! Lunar Outpost aims to deploy the first GPU on the lunar surface using Jetson technology for advanced robotic exploration.
summary: Nvidia is deploying its Jetson GPU platform for lunar exploration, positioning it as a core component for future space infrastructure. Lunar Outpost plans to use these chips to control its next moon rover's lidar system, potentially marking the first GPU on the lunar surface. This effort aligns with NASA's goal of preparatory exploration ahead of human return missions, estimated for as soon as 2028. The Jetson platform is crucial because its compact, power-efficient design allows autonomous rovers to process sensor data locally, improving decision-making in challenging environments. Operating in the extreme conditions of the Moon, which faces cosmic radiation and temperature swings, requires advanced, specialized hardware. The technology was further showcased through a partnership between Nvidia and Firefly Aerospace, which will use the Jetson platform on a satellite orbiting the moon to map and track scientific data.
author: Tim Fernholz
content: Nvidia's effort to deploy its GPUs far and wide is aiming at a new target: the moon. Lunar Outpost , a startup building robotics for space infrastructure, announced on Thursday that its next moon rover will use Jetson chips to control its lidar system. When it does, it is likely to be the first GPU on the lunar surface. "We're taking the Nvidia Jetson and comparing it to our flight compute platform that has a little bit more spaceflight heritage," Lunar Outpost CEO Justin Cyrus said. "[We're] seeing what the pros are, seeing what the cons are. And we're really pushing towards trying to adopt these more capable GPU-powered systems in these extreme environments." NASA has launched a campaign to pay private companies to explore the lunar surface ahead of plans to return human astronauts, perhaps as soon as 2028. The space agency's program, modeled on its work with SpaceX, asks tech companies to develop vehicles that carry scientific sensors to the moon to understand its terrain and hunt for substances like water that could prove useful or even lucrative to exploit. Nvidia also recently announced a partnership with Firefly Aerospace, the first private company to safely land a robot on the moon, that will see the Jetson platform operate on a satellite orbiting the moon to process imagery. That satellite aims to collect data for scientists trying to map the moon, but also to track the growing number of robots on the surface. Lunar Outpost's next rover is packaged onboard a lander built by Intuitive Machines, another moon-focused tech company. The rover is designed to carry a package of sensors into craters and other places that are difficult to explore from orbit. The following mission will be exploring a place on the lunar surface called Reiner Gamma, where a magnetic anomaly has puzzled scientists. Each mission is expected to take flight on a Falcon 9 rocket before the end of the year. Nvidia's Jetson platform isn't as well known as AI workhorses like Blackwell and Vera Rubin, but it's a vital part of many physical AI systems. Designed to be compact and power-efficient, Jetson lets robotic systems process sensor inputs locally, allowing them to understand and react to the world around them more quickly. "Our autonomy stack was a bit more deterministic five years ago, and now it's a combination of deterministic and physical AI, which is pretty fun," Cyrus said. "We still run both in parallel, and then it's our job to figure out where physical AI can actually plug into our stack and help us do things that no one's done before." Using GPUs in space is challenging because of the extreme environment. Most space-faring GPUs are in orbit close to the Earth, where they are relatively protected from radiation and dramatic temperature changes. The moon is more directly exposed to cosmic radiation and swings in temperature as it goes through its phases. "Your system has to survive lunar night and has to do so on very low power," Cyrus said. If they can operate the chips in that environment, Lunar Outpost's engineers hope that their vehicles will be more capable - able to more quickly process their environment and make decisions. NASA has extensive ambitions for a sustained human presence on the moon, but that will likely require autonomous systems to pave the way and do the heavy lifting. "What we at Lunar Outpost are currently working on is how do we go from exploration to permanence, how do we actually build that outpost on the moon?" Cyrus said. "We do think combining our deterministic models plus the physical AI layer - that's what allows us to make a human presence in space sustainable, actually having that robotic workforce." In the next few years, Lunar Outpost has several smaller autonomous rovers scheduled for launch to the moon, and one larger one, Pegasus, that is intended to carry astronauts. Pegasus is waiting on a rocket built by Jeff Bezos' space company, Blue Origin, to carry it to the moon, but that launch vehicle suffered an anomaly this summer and it's not clear when it will return to flight. "It does seem like they're making pretty darn good progress on the pad," Cyrus said. "I can't really answer Blue Origin's timelines or NASA's timelines on the pad reconstruction, but everything we've been told, we're on the same timeline [for 2028]." That leaves futuristic visions of space data centers and fleets of robots at work on the moon both waiting on the same thing: a bigger rocket.

title: The new Halo remake is a reminder of what Xbox used to be
teaser: Despite delivering a brilliant return to form, Halo: Campaign Evolved launches into a troubled era for Xbox, highlighting the franchise's tenuous state.
summary: Halo: Campaign Evolved, a modern reimagining built on Unreal Engine 5, revives the classic sci-fi shooter experience. Players once again step into Master Chief's boots, fighting the Covenant and the terrifying Flood. While the remake enhances the core action with upgraded visuals, making areas grander and the Flood encounters scarier, it introduces key quality-of-life improvements like a sprint button and vehicle hijacking. Despite the game's excellent execution, its release highlights the current turbulence of Xbox, which faces layoffs and strategic uncertainty. The title launches on the Xbox, PS5, and PC on July 28th, offering fans a brilliant return to form amidst the console's struggles.
author: Andrew Webster
content: It's impossible to talk about a new Xbox game without also talking about the state of Xbox. Microsoft's gaming division is in freefall: Recent headlines are dominated by extensive layoffs , decimated studios , and confusing strategies , most of which stem from years of bad decisions and expensive acquisitions . But it wasn't always that way. Through its first two generations of existence, Xbox held its own against its more established rivals Nintendo and Sony, and a big reason for that was Halo . Bungie's shooter coupled a grand sci-fi story with nearly pitch-perfect action and single-handedly created a reason to buy an Xbox. Now, the game has gotten a full remake, reimagining the same core experience for modern audiences. In a testament to the original design, Halo remains a thrilling game more than two decades after it debuted. But the remake is also a reminder of just how far Xbox has strayed from its initial promise. Called Halo: Campaign Evolved , the remake is exactly what it sounds like: a modern overhaul of the original game's story campaign. That means you still take on the role of supersoldier Master Chief as he leads human forces in a war against an alien alliance known as the Covenant, before eventually being pulled into a much bigger conflict with the fate of the galaxy on the line. Halo 's story was never the most original, pulling from obvious influences, most notably Aliens , but it's well crafted, with dramatic twists and turns that give you an incentive to push through its many battles. The game is especially great at switching tones throughout. Initially Halo puts you on the front lines of a large-scale war on an alien world before later shifting to something that approaches horror, with cramped shootouts against unsettling monsters. Campaign Evolved makes the story a touch more cinematic with expanded cutscenes that flesh out the backstory and characters, but which are still relatively short and concise. The most notable difference in the remake is its upgraded visuals. Campaign Evolved was built using Unreal Engine 5, and it looks, well, like a first-person shooter from 2026. Everything is much more detailed and the levels are grander in scope. When you're out on the Halo's surface, it really feels like you're in the midst of a huge battle, with explosions all around you and the wreckage of downed vehicles and ships dotting the landscape. That extra level of detail really enhances the game midway through when you encounter the Flood, a race of parasitic aliens that turn corpses into zombies. Now those close-quarters battles are much scarier, as the aliens explode in gruesome ways, the walls are covered with oozing growths, and you see the flash of gunfire lighting up dark spaces and the horrors lurking within. You can quibble with some of the artistic decisions - I personally miss the more brutalist alien architecture of the original - but overall the game looks great. There are changes to the gameplay as well. Some are relatively small, like the new ability to hijack enemy vehicles or the larger arsenal of weapons at your disposal. The biggest change, though, is something that seems small: the addition of a sprint button. Early Halo games didn't let Master Chief sprint, and the addition to Campaign Evolved makes the action feel much faster and more fluid. It's especially useful if, like me, you spend a lot of time running away from the bigger enemies. Campaign Evolved also introduces a trio of new missions while making some changes to existing ones. Unfortunately, I don't have the kind of encyclopedic Halo knowledge to pinpoint exactly what has changed, but I will say this: Much like the remakes of Shadow of the Colossus and Resident Evil 4 , Campaign Evolved plays the romanticized version of Halo from my memory, which is exactly what you want from a project like this. The changes enhance something that was already great and smooth over (most of) the rough spots. And while I played through all of it solo, the game also supports co-op for up to four players. While the remake is excellent, it's unfortunately launching at a very awkward time, just a few weeks after new Xbox CEO Asha Sharma kicked off a "reset" that will eventually see more than 3,000 people laid off over the next year and iconic studios like Doom developer id Software dramatically scaled down. In many ways, Halo as a franchise is illustrative of Xbox's fall from grace. Since Microsoft assumed full responsibility for the series through its internal Halo Studios (formerly known as 343 Industries), the gap between new releases has become larger and larger, while at the same time the company has tried to broaden Halo through mostly ill-fated ventures like a streaming TV series and a live-service push . Campaign Evolved itself represents some of this disorder. Not only is it the first new Halo game since 2021, it's also coming to the PS5 in addition to Xbox and PC as part of Microsoft's consistently confusing console exclusivity strategy . So as much as I've enjoyed fighting off the hordes of the Flood once again, I can't help but see Campaign Evolved within the larger context of Xbox. The original Halo felt daring, proving that action and narrative could be complementary strengths, and it went on to influence a generation of first-person shooters. In the years since, the franchise's prominence has steadily diminished, to the point that now Microsoft is trying to reinvigorate it by going back to the beginning instead of doing something actually new. Five years after Halo Infinite , instead of the next entry in the franchise, Xbox has opted for the safe choice with a remake. And Campaign Evolved comes at a time when the future of the Xbox lineup looks increasingly murky given the dramatic studio cuts. Campaign Evolved does a remarkable job of re-creating the experience of playing Halo for the first time. But that's not enough to make Halo - or Xbox, for that matter - feel as essential as it once was. Halo: Campaign Evolved launches on the Xbox, PS5, and PC on July 28th, with early access on July 23rd for those who preordered . Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. Andrew Webster Entertainment Games Review Gaming Xbox

title: Reddit Weighs Tighter Google AI Data Access in Deal Renewal Talks
teaser: Google's AI models depend on Reddit's structured data feed, as the companies renegotiate a major $60 million license renewal.
summary: Reddit and Google are in renewal talks for a $60 million annual license for Reddit's data, critical for training Google's Gemini AI models. Under the paid agreement, Google receives a structured, real-time feed of posts and comments, which offers benefits like fresh data and consistent delivery compared to simple public web crawling. Reddit is leveraging its value to push for tighter access control and better compensation, arguing that its data's structured nature is key. Potential outcomes include revised pricing, stricter usage terms, or even a rejection of the renewal, though Reddit's Q1 revenue of $663 million supports its negotiating position.
author: Markus Kasanmascheff
content: TL;DR Renewal Talks: Reddit is weighing tighter Google AI access while the companies discuss renewing a reported $60 million annual license. Structured Data: Google receives real-time, organized Reddit posts and comments for model training, product improvements and content displays. Access Limits: Paid API access and public crawling are separate, so narrower licensed access does not remove every public Reddit page. Results Checkpoint: Reddit's scheduled second-quarter results give executives a chance to discuss renewal without guaranteeing a licensing announcement. Reddit is weighing tighter AI data access for Google as the companies discuss renewing their $60 million annual license . Both a cutoff and a rejection of renewal remain possibilities, not final decisions, after details became public on July 22. A possible renewal of Google's AI content deal remains under discussion as the annual license approaches its end. Google currently receives a controlled feed of structured Reddit posts and comments for products including its Gemini AI models. Reddit's paid-access stance dates to 2024. By June 2025, Reddit was a top source in Google's AI Overviews, illustrating why a controlled feed of structured Reddit posts and comments matters to AI products. A reported 8% drop in Reddit shares accompanied the possible restriction becoming public on July 22. Reddit wants partnerships to support its business and recognize the value of its data, while deal-specific Google renewal terms are not public. Tighter access, revised pricing and an extension remain possible outcomes rather than settled decisions. What Google Gets From Reddit's Data Feed Google obtained programmatic access to public posts and comments under the original paid-data agreement signed in February 2024. Its terms reflected Reddit's insistence that technology companies pay for data use . A programmatic feed lets Google receive organized data directly rather than relying only on scraping ordinary public web pages. Google gained real-time, structured access that supports displays of Reddit material, product improvements and model training. Model training uses examples to shape an AI system's learned behavior. Organized data supplies fresher information and enhanced signals, reducing the work required to ingest conversations and helping products reflect newer language. Because the Data API supplies organized content, structured delivery gives Google's systems a consistent route for posts and comments instead of requiring each product to gather the same material separately. Defined purposes and permissions can make that access more predictable for product teams. Delivery speed and structure have operational value beyond the raw availability of public text. Google can use the feed both to improve models and to display Reddit material in its products. Those uses depend on organized delivery, while access to public crawlable pages operates through a separate mechanism. Because commercial use requires Reddit's approval , Reddit retained control over the licensed feed. Reddit can tie permission to purpose and contract terms, then price automated commercial access. Even if Reddit narrows paid API access, Google's 2024 terms did not change crawlable-content use for indexing, training or display. A restriction could reduce Gemini's structured stream of Reddit data without removing every public Reddit page from Google's systems. Revised terms could change price, permitted purposes, delivery speed or data structure, while slower or less organized delivery could affect freshness and processing work. Reddit's Leverage and the Next Test AI-generated answers have intensified disputes over publisher compensation and traffic, with earlier research finding AI summaries reducing referral clicks . Reddit entered the talks after first-quarter 2026 revenue was reported 69% higher year over year at $663 million , while earnings per share reached $1.01 against an expected 58 cents. Referral pressure has not been established as the cause of Reddit's position, and the Google partnership remains important to Reddit. In 2025, the company pushed for dynamic pricing that could tie compensation more closely to the value Google receives. Reddit's leverage comes from controlling the delivery channel and its permission rules, while public crawling does not reproduce the API's structure, freshness or contractually defined uses. A higher price could buy predictable delivery, while tighter conditions or usage-based payments could protect Reddit's control without surrendering licensing income. Reddit will report second-quarter results on July 30. Leadership will then probalbly clarify whether the structured feed will continue, although the results call does not guarantee a licensing announcement.

title: Microsoft is testing free, ad-supported cloud gaming for Xbox Insiders
teaser: Xbox Insiders can now stream owned games for free via a new, limited ad-supported cloud gaming test.
summary: Microsoft is testing an ad-supported, free cloud gaming model for Xbox Insiders, allowing them to stream their owned games for up to one hour. Ads are limited to pre-session viewing. This move reflects a broader industry trend toward ad monetization and aims to expand affordable ways to play Xbox titles, potentially helping Xbox One owners play games built for newer consoles. This test is part of Xbox’s efforts to stabilize its service model, notably after increasing unlimited cloud gaming access to the $9.99 Game Pass Essential tier. The news comes as Xbox faces turmoil, including pending console price increases of over $100 starting August 1st.
author: Stevie Bonifield
content: Xbox Insiders can stream games from their libraries for free in ad-supported streaming sessions starting today. The free streaming sessions are limited to games you already own, and sessions are capped at one hour. However, ads will only play "before sessions begin." It's also optional - you won't need to watch ads if you have a paid cloud gaming subscription. Microsoft says the ad-supported streaming option will only be available for a limited time during a "test period." It previously began internally testing an ad-supported version of Xbox Cloud Gaming late last year, with sources telling The Verge at the time that the test included about two minutes of preroll ads before streaming sessions. Around the same time, Microsoft also increased Game Pass prices , but added unlimited cloud gaming to its lowest-priced Game Pass Essential subscription, which costs $9.99 per month. Previously, you needed a Game Pass Ultimate subscription for Xbox Cloud Gaming. Microsoft says the goal of its current test for ad-supported streaming is to further expand affordable ways to play Xbox games. Ad tiers have become increasingly common on video streaming platforms over recent years - the addition of ads on Xbox's streaming service could signal a similar shift coming to gaming subscriptions. Additionally, Microsoft notes that cloud gaming could "help Xbox One owners play newer games built for Xbox Series X/S" without needing to buy a new console. The news comes as Xbox is in a state of upheaval , including mass layoffs , studio closures , and a pivot back toward the fan-favorite Fallout franchise. On top of that, Xbox console prices are set to increase by upwards of $100 starting on August 1st.

title: Meta launched a new AI optimism ad set to a song about human extinction
teaser: From Bowie's mass-extinction anthem to cemetery imagery: AI firms battle for trust with contradictory ad campaigns.
summary: Major AI companies are locked in a marketing battle to control public perception of artificial intelligence. Meta ran an 'optimism' ad using David Bowie's 'Five Years,' a song about human extinction, creating a jarring contrast. Meanwhile, rival Anthropic released a doomerist ad ('There's hope in hard questions') featuring imagery like facial recognition surveillance, mines, and cemeteries, attempting to position itself as the ethical AI leader. Experts note that these contradictory marketing stunts are signs of the industry's struggle to convince the public, especially given that a Pew survey found only 16% of Americans predict a positive AI impact.
author: Amanda Silberling
content: Meta's newest advertisement begins with a black-and-white shot of an eye, showing us what someone sees as they read countless panicked headlines about how AI is going to take our jobs, isolate us, and spark a global crisis. "Some people will have you believe AI is going to make us feel less connected. That it's going to leave us behind," a voiceover says. "We couldn't disagree more." Suddenly, the video shifts to color, and shows a cycle of different people opening their eyes and smiling. Then, we see a couple dancing on a rooftop, pointing at a rainbow; a group of teens swimming in a lake; a child frolicking in a field; friends embracing after time apart. "Call us optimists. Call us dreamers. Call us whatever the hell you want. But we're betting on people, and we like those odds," the voiceover says. "The future is for everyone." That's a nice sentiment - pretty convenient for a company betting hundreds of billions of dollars that AI will revolutionize humanity. But the strangest part of the advertisement is not that we're watching these happy moments play out via Instagram posts. It's that the soundtrack to the ad is the David Bowie song "Five Years." If you are not familiar with this song, I urge you to give it a listen , read the lyrics , and think about what it is trying to say. It seems clear to me, but I studied poetry in college, so as a control for this experiment, I asked my brother - a blockchain analyst who loves Claude Code and does not read for fun - if he could tell me what the song is about. "I thought climate change at first, then zombie apocalypse, then an asteroid hitting the earth," he told me. He is correct. It is a song about the human race panicking after learning they will die in a mass-extinction event in five years. Image Credits: Texts from my brother, a consenting participant in this literary experiment If you're not familiar with Bowie's music, this track might sound happy and inspiring, matching the ad's upbeat tone. The part of the song that is used for the advertisement was probably chosen because it uses the word "people" over and over again, and without the context of the song, it's not clear what it's about. But if we look at the lines directly preceding this section: News had just come over We had five years left to cry in News guy wept and told us Earth was really dying Cried so much his face was wet Then I knew he was not lying We "had five years left to cry in" and the "earth was really dying." It's pretty bleak. It is not reassuring to convince people that AI is going to make the world better while playing a song about the end of the world, and yet, this contradictory musical choice seems to have sailed right past everyone at Meta, including CEO Mark Zuckerberg. "Meta has always believed in giving people the power to share, connect, and shape your world in the ways you want," he wrote alongside the video. "As we enter this next wave with AI, we continue to believe the future is for everyone. We're focused on giving every person the tools to reach your full potential and making sure the benefits of technology are distributed to everyone." Then again, tech leaders are not known for their literary analysis skills. Meta's Oculus used to give new hires copies of the science fiction novel " Ready Player One ," which is set in a dystopia in which a tech company making virtual reality products becomes overly powerful and evil. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has directly cited inspiration from the movie "Her," which warns us about what can go wrong when we use AI for emotional support . Palantir, a company that builds AI surveillance systems for the government, is named after Palantir, a seeing stone from the "Lord of the Rings" franchise that the Dark Lord uses to spy on his enemies. Elon Musk is currently throwing a fit about the "accuracy" of Christopher Nolan's blockbuster adaptation of "The Odyssey," a story with such realistic elements as sea monsters, magic, and divine intervention. These guys make a great argument for the value of studying the humanities. Meta isn't alone in its recent promotional foibles. Instead of racing to build AGI, the top AI companies seem to be fighting over who can make the creepiest advertisement. A few weeks ago, Anthropic released an eerie video of its own. As my colleague Lucas Ropek described it: The ad begins with a video of a burning house (not exactly a heartwarming start) before pivoting to a series of still images. These images include a crowd of people being surveilled by facial recognition, a homeless person sleeping on the street, rows upon rows of tombstones in a cemetery, and what appears to be a group of laborers toiling in a mine where (presumably) raw materials for smartphones are being dug up. Meanwhile, a voice-over track features different people asking questions like "Can AI be trusted?" and "Who's gonna hit the brakes if we need to?" Anthropic is trying to convince us that it understands the risks AI poses to society, and therefore, this is the company that people can trust to develop AI responsibly. The message it actually conveys feels closer to the mood of Bowie's "Five Years." OpenAI CEO Sam Altman responded to the Anthropic ad, "I thought this was satire, kept looking for the handle to be spelled c1audeai or something." As these companies spar to control the public perception of AI, their efforts don't seem to be making much progress. A recent Pew survey found that only 16% of Americans think that AI's impact on society over the next 20 years will be positive, and 40% believe it will have a negative impact. Better luck next time, Meta.

title: OpenAI makes ChatGPT Health available to all US users
teaser: OpenAI expands ChatGPT Health to all US users, allowing them to integrate medical records and health data into general chat queries.
summary: OpenAI is rolling out ChatGPT Health to all US users, enabling the chatbot to draw insights from connected personal health information in the general chat, moving beyond the dedicated health hub. Users can now link medical records from systems like Epic and Oracle Health, alongside data from services such as Apple Health and MyFitnessPal. This major update allows general questions to incorporate specific, connected health details. The service, running on models like GPT-5.6-Luna, supports professional care by providing advanced assistance, though OpenAI stresses that its services are 'not intended for use in the diagnosis or treatment of any health condition.' This rollout follows a lawsuit and emphasizes that users must verify all medical advice with professionals. The feature is now available across all US plans (free, Go, Plus, and Pro) on web and iOS.
author: Ivan Mehta
content: OpenAI said today it is making ChatGPT Health, a feature that helps users with health-related queries, available to all U.S.-based users over 18 across all plans. The announcement comes a day after a Florida-based pastor sued the company for giving a near-fatal suggestion not to consult a doctor . The company started testing the feature through a dedicated hub earlier in January, allowing users to integrate data from other services and their personal information from services such as Apple Health, Function, and MyFitnessPal. At that time, OpenAI said users were asking 230 million health-related queries each week. That number has now gone up to 300 million. ChatGPT health Image Credits: OpenAI Users can also integrate their medical records from hospital systems like Epic and Oracle Health, and health platforms like One Medical and Function Health. OpenAI said earlier that users needed to use the health hub for health-related queries. Now they can choose to draw insights from connected information in the health section in all queries. The company said during the testing it observed that 70% of health-related queries took place outside the dedicated hub. Through this new feature, users can use their health information to get information on food or allergies in the general chat. The company noted that its models have made progress in answering health-related queries. The company noted that the smallest model from its latest release, GPT 5.6-Luna, outperforms GPT 5.5 on HealthBench evaluation, an open source benchmark developed by the company to evaluate large language models (LLMs) on health queries . OpenAI said that it doesn't use any user data to train its model, and it works with physicians to improve its models on health queries. Despite these performance gains, the company maintains in its terms that its services are "not intended for use in the diagnosis or treatment of any health condition." The company cited these clauses in response to the above lawsuit, and also told The New York Times that it is working on making health- or medicine-related answers safer. With the latest roll out, OpenAI said it wants people to verify information and take medical decisions based on professional advice. Several studies have highlighted that AI bots are not reliable for medical advice. However, this has not deterred companies like Anthropic and Google from launching health-related AI features. Health in ChatGPT is rolling out to logged-in U.S. users with free, Go, Plus, and Pro plans on the web and iOS this week.

title: Tesla’s robotaxi promises are clashing with reality
teaser: Tesla's ambitious robotaxi promises clash with reality: mileages are flat, and a competitor drives 5x more per week.
summary: Despite CEO Elon Musk's bullish projections, Tesla's robotaxi program faces significant skepticism regarding its actual growth and safety. While Tesla's AI head, Ashok Elluswamy, touted the system's generalizability using only cameras—challenging the industry need for lidar—the data suggests stagnation. For instance, Tesla's total mileage is less than 10% of Waymo’s weekly output (around four million miles). Furthermore, regulatory concerns, such as New Jersey considering a ban on multi-sensor-lacking robots, limit the addressable market. Safety is another concern, as the Full Self-Driving system is under NHTSA investigation, contradicting claims of flawless expansion.
author: Andrew J. Hawkins
content: In an earnings call yesterday , Tesla CEO Elon Musk did his best to paint a positive portrait of the company's robotaxi program. New cities are being added, more miles are being driven, and more people are experiencing Tesla's unsupervised vehicles. But Musk's typical bullishness seemed to be absent from the call, as the occasional trillionaire sought to temper expectations about the program's future. "We're going as fast as humanly possible in scaling Robotaxi," Musk said, "while trying to ensure that we do not harm anyone at all and ideally do not even run over a pet." Musk's insistence that Tesla's robotaxi service was growing is clashing with the reality of the situation: Mileage is basically flat , the number of vehicles appears to be shrinking, and despite the Tesla executive team's claims of "zero notable incidents," the safety of the company's technology appears to be an open question. Tesla did it's best to frame the situation as headed in the right direction. Ashok Elluswamy, the company's head of AI, said that Tesla's unsupervised robotaxis have driven 380,000 miles across six cities in two different states. And according to Musk, that was increasing at a rate of 10 percent a week in terms of miles driven. Tesla did it's best to frame the situation as headed in the right direction Elluswamy couldn't help but take a swipe at Tesla's competitors who use lidar sensors, as opposed to Tesla's camera-0nly approach. "Historically, the so-called experts have always claimed that you need lidars, radars, HD maps, and the entire kitchen sink to drive safely," he said. "Here we show that such is not true. You can have safe, comfortable, and affordable autonomy with just cameras. This record should be a huge validation of Tesla's entire AI approach." But even the numbers that Tesla reported seem to betray that message. Waymo, which uses lidar sensors and radar as redundant sensors in addition to cameras, typically drives around four million miles a week. Tesla's total mileage, a year into its robotaxi program, is less than 10 percent of that figure. This reality is starting to spook investors, with BNP Paribas Equity Research senior analyst James Picariello calling it "an alarming decline" in a research note to clients. Tesla uses a mix of unsupervised and supervised vehicles as part of its fleet, but that ratio appears to be in a constant state of flux. According to the crowdsourced Robotaxi Tracker , the company currently only has 16 unsupervised vehicles in Austin, four in Dallas, and one in Houston. During the earnings call, Elluswamy was asked what was preventing Tesla from flooding the zone in Austin, where it first launched its robotaxis a year ago, as opposed to dropping a small number of vehicles in new cities. "The reason we have been expanding across different cities, instead of just doubling down on a single city, is that we want to make sure that our stack is a very general one," Elluswamy said. "It is a general one. We just want to like, you know, both prove to ourselves and to other folks that it is working across a lot of different cities without too much effort per city." Another limiting factor is state regulations. New Jersey is considering a bill that would essentially ban robotaxis without multiple sensors, like radar and lidar. Morgan Stanley analyst Andrew Percoco flagged this on the call, noting "there seems to be some evolving regulations at the state level, potentially around sensor requirements." To which Tesla's vice president of vehicle engineering Lars Morvay acknowledged "obviously the stuff in New Jersey, you know, is a little bit disheartening." A more restrictive regulatory environment could limit the total addressable market for Tesla robotaxis, which would clash with the company's message about a more generalized service that can drive anywhere, under any conditions. Safety is another obstacle. Musk's comment about wanting to avoid running over anyone's pet appeared to be a subtle swipe at Waymo, which has hit and killed a number of animals over the past several years. But Tesla's safety record is a mixed bag. We don't have a lot of great insight into Tesla's robotaxi crashes because the company tends to redact a lot of the important details. According to the Robotaxi Tracker, the company's fleet has been involved in approximately 18 incidents, 56 percent of which were the fault of another driver. And Tesla's Full Self-Driving is under investigation by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, with the potential for a future recall. Tesla's robotaxis are currently running version 15 of FSD, as compared to version 14.3.6 on its customer vehicles. Tesla is asking investors, supporters, and customers to look past these shortcomings as it continues to push the message that it's robotaxi program is growing. But the company continues to run into a reality that contradicts that message. title: Anthropic updates Claude voice mode with more capable models
teaser: Anthropic updates Claude voice mode to use Opus and Sonnet models, giving users the power to write emails, manage calendars, and do deep analysis hands-free.
summary: Rival Anthropic has significantly upgraded its Claude voice mode, moving beyond simple chat to facilitate complex, actionable tasks. Users can now select from three models—Haiku, Sonnet, or Opus—allowing them to transition from quick chats to deep, professional problem-solving. The new voice mode greatly expands integration with popular apps like Gmail, Slack, and Notion, enabling users to draft emails, update calendars, or create documents hands-free. Furthermore, multilingual support has been broadened across several languages, providing a powerful, versatile tool for business and research.
author: Ivan Mehta
content: Weeks after OpenAI rolled out a new family of conversational models and updated ChatGPT's voice mode , rival Anthropic is making its move to make Claude more voice-friendly with a new update. The company said Thursday that users can choose between Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku models. Claude's voice mode, which was released last year and powered by the Haiku model, provided quick responses, but wasn't well suited for complex work. The company said that with the new update, voice mode picks the last model people used in the text chat and uses its fastest version by default. Anthropic said that the new voice mode can help users with longer conversations, including providing feedback on their communication style, talking through a pitch to a client, and brainstorming product market research. Image Credits: Anthropic What's more, Claude's voice mode can tap into other apps like Gmail, Google Calendar, Slack, Canva, and Notion. This means that users can ask it to update a meeting slot, draft an email, or create a document in Notion. Notably, this is a big difference from OpenAI's voice mode, which updated its conversational style but still isn't able to use different tools to get work done. Image Credits: Anthropic Earlier this year, Anthropic added multilingual support to Claude's voice mode in beta. It said that now users can talk in various languages, but they have to manually specify the language. At the moment, Anthropic supports English, French, German, Hindi, Indonesian, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese (Brazilian), and Spanish (Latin America/Spain). The new voice mode is available to all users in beta across platforms. However, free users will be restricted to using the Haiku model with only one connected app. Anthropic didn't make any changes to the voice model with this release, and it hasn't detailed what kind of voice stack it uses. That means, unlike OpenAI's release, users might not find any conversational improvements such as better interruption handling.

title: FCC Chairman Brendan Carr’s war on the First Amendment
teaser: FCC Chairman Brendan Carr is pushing to end a limit that prevents one company from owning too many local TV stations, sparking concerns about local journalism's future.
summary: The FCC and its Chairman, Brendan Carr, are embroiled in a debate over ending the national ownership cap rule for broadcast television. This rule was designed to prevent media monopolies by limiting how many local stations one company could own (currently capped at 39% of US TV households). Carr argues that modern platforms like social media make this limit obsolete and restricts competition from national programmers. If repealed, proponents argue it allows scale comparable to their streaming rivals. However, opponents warn that eliminating the cap could harm vital local journalism by reducing necessary competition. Democratic Commissioner Anna Gomez questioned if the FCC has the authority to eliminate a limit set by Congress, suggesting only Congress can make such changes.
author: Kevin Nguyen
content: As the chairman of the Federal Communications Commission, Brendan Carr has authority over the nation's TV, radio, and internet. But since Donald Trump was elected to his second term, Carr has wielded that power to threaten broadcasters that have exercised their free speech rights to make jokes about the president. He was even able to get ABC to briefly pull Jimmy Kimmel from his late-night show. As The Verge editor-in-chief Nilay Patel has said , Carr's mission is to "trash the First Amendment." We'll be following closely as the FCC chairman attempts to erode Americans' constitutional rights.
