title: Tesla’s door handles may spur new US safety rules
teaser: Tragedy strikes: NHTSA is opening a rule-making process to overhaul car door handles after multiple incidents left occupants trapped inside vehicles.
summary: U.S. regulators, specifically the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), are investigating new federal safety rules for vehicle door handles and emergency exits. This action follows several high-profile incidents—some fatal—where occupants became trapped in vehicles equipped with flush, electronically operated door handles, like those found on Tesla models. NHTSA has initiated a rulemaking process to address the risk of occupant entrapment, particularly during electrical power failures. While NHTSA noted that granting the petition only 'commences' the process and doesn't guarantee new standards, the agency is gathering data to determine if a new safety rule is necessary. These rules, if adopted, would apply to all automakers, affecting the design of mechanical door releases and internal handle placement.
author: Kirsten Korosec
content: U.S. regulators will look into developing new requirements for automakers to ensure drivers and passengers can safely exit their vehicles. The new rule-making process, outlined in a regulatory filing and first reported by Bloomberg , follows a series of incidents, including fatal ones, in which people have become stuck inside cars with flush, electronically operated door handles like those found on Tesla vehicles. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) made the announcement in response to a petition that asked the agency to open a safety defect investigation into the emergency mechanical door release design on 2022 Tesla Model 3 vehicles. The petition argued that door release doesn't comply with federal motor vehicle standards. NHTSA denied taking the action that the petitioners wanted, saying that the issue would be best addressed through rule-making rather than a defect investigation. If the agency adopts new rules, all automakers will need to follow them. However, it's important to note that "commencing" rulemaking doesn't mean new ones will be developed, according to NHTSA. "NHTSA received a petition for rulemaking to require an emergency door egress system to address the risk of occupant entrapment in vehicles during electrical power failures, and the agency granted that petition," the agency explained in an emailed statement. "Granting a rulemaking petition is not a decision by NHTSA to issue a new safety standard, but commences the process of gathering input to make an informed decision. NHTSA will gather additional information and data, and solicit public comments, to determine if a rulemaking for a new safety standard is appropriate under the requirements of the Vehicle Safety Act." The decision comes less than a year after NHTSA opened an investigation into Tesla's door handles after receiving nine reports from owners who were unable to get into their cars, sometimes with children still inside. The probe followed Bloomberg's own investigation into a series of incidents in which Tesla drivers and passengers became trapped inside their vehicles following a crash. While Tesla vehicles do have manual door releases, they are located only inside the car. In an initial review by NHTSA, investigators found the handles may not work if the electronic door locks don't receive enough voltage from the vehicle's battery system. Tesla designer Franz von Holzhausen said last year that the company was working on a redesign of its door handles. Rivian said last year it was changing the interior door handle design on its R2 SUV to put the manual release in a more visible location, closer to the electrically powered door handles. This article was updated to include a statement from NHTSA.

title: Insurance startup Corgi reportedly raised more money at $4B — its third round in 8 weeks
teaser: In a flurry of funding, insurance tech startup Corgi is reportedly raising a B2 round, valuing the company potentially at $4B.
summary: Corgi, an AI-powered insurance tech startup, is reportedly engaged in a rapid cycle of funding, rumored to be raising a B2 round after previous successful raises, reaching a $2.6 billion valuation in its B1 round. Its growth is fueled by its projected revenue run rate, which is expected to hit $450 million by year-end. Corgi's core model uses Risk Retention Groups (RRGs)—a self-insurance pool less regulated than traditional carriers. Beyond insurance, the company has diversified by offering data room software and operating physical coffee shops. The company's explosive growth and complex business structure position it as a prominent, yet highly ambitious, player in the insurtech space.
author: Julie Bort
content: Insurance tech, data room software, and coffee-shop startup Corgi is reportedly raising yet another round that closely follows its last raise and would double its valuation, sources have told Forbes . The round is said to be a second extension of its Series B round and has already closed. Corgi announced its last round, the B1 round of $106 million at a $2.6 billion valuation at the end of May, about eight weeks ago. In the AI-funding frenzy, many startups are raising back-to-back rounds at ever-increasing valuations - but even by those standards, Corgi stands out. The Y Combinator alum (summer 2024) raised a $108 million Series A in January at an undisclosed valuation. (PitchBook estimates $630 million post-money.) Four months later, in early May, it raised its Series B : $160 million at a $1.3 billion valuation. Just three weeks later, it announced a B1 round from the same investors, saying they'd invested $106 million at a $2.6 billion valuation. Now, eight weeks later, sources tell Forbes there's a B2. Forbes did not report the amount of money that Corgi raised, though, and the company declined to comment on the potential funding. Corgi is backed by TCV and Kindred Ventures. Kindred's Kanyi Maqubela cited the startup's momentum to TechCrunch as justification for the last valuation leap. The apparent justification for the new valuation is the startup's revenue trajectory. When Corgi announced its Series A seven months ago, the founders said their company had already hit $40 million in annualized revenue run rate . Sources told Forbes it's now on track to increase run rate to $450 million by the end of the year. Corgi offers AI-powered insurance. It uses AI to give prospects fast quotes and to speed payments on claims . It offers startups various types of liability insurance like general liability, coverage of tech-related incidents, and employment liability, as well as business renters' and auto insurance. Insurance is an inherently cash-intensive business but perhaps even more so for Corgi because it uses a type of insurance structure known as a Risk Retention Group (RRG). This is a way for people in the same industry, or those facing similar liabilities, to pool their resources and self-insure collectively. According to Corgi's website , RRGs aren't subject to all the same state regulations as traditional, rated, underwritten insurance carriers. Corgi has adopted some different structures for different types of insurance, however, a spokesperson says. In addition to RRGs, some policies might use state-regulated carriers, for instance. However, in an RRG insurance business, claims are paid out of the pool, and a steep claim can impact how much is left in the kitty to pay other claims. RRGs aren't backed by state guaranty funds, so if the pool can't pay, members bear the loss. If the claims are big enough, they can even bankrupt the RRG . Perhaps it's not surprising, then, that Corgi wants to grow its coffers. But even as the startup has expanded the types of insurance it offers, it has also branched out in other ways. Corgi now offers data room software , having weathered a recent uproar over how that software was vibe coded. Plus, the startup operates two 24-hour coffee shops with cute and sometimes ad-sponsored drink names like "Brexspresso." Its shops are located in San Francisco and Atlanta, but it says it's planning to launch five more soon, including several in New York and one in London. Opening up physical cafe locations also requires cash. Meanwhile, Corgi has a reputation in Silicon Valley for having a demanding corporate culture after founder-CEO Nico Laqua said he expects his employees to work seven days a week.

title: Patreon lays off 20% of its workforce
teaser: The AI revolution is reshaping corporate structure: Tech giants like Patreon and Monday.com cut 20% of their workforce to invest heavily in artificial intelligence platforms.
summary: Major tech players like Patreon and Monday.com are undergoing significant restructuring and layoffs, primarily citing the need to adapt to market changes driven by artificial intelligence. Patreon cut 20% of its staff (93 people) and is protecting creators' work by partnering with Cloudflare to block AI bots from scraping content. Similarly, Monday.com cut 20% of its staff (about 630) to concentrate resources on its AI Work Platform. These trends reflect a wider industry pattern, as data indicates that a record 78% of companies are blaming the need to focus on AI as the reason for job cuts, contributing to over 122,000 tech roles being cut in 2026.
author: Aisha Malik
content: Patreon is laying off 20% of its workforce, or 93 people, CEO Jack Conte told employees on Thursday. In a memo to staff that was shared online by the company, Conte said Patreon's core business is strong but that the platform has to respond to market changes and adjust its cost structure to remain stable, which is why it needs to make the "painful" but necessary cuts. Conte wrote that "AI has fundamentally transformed the tech industry," and that the pace of change has "never been more intense." However, Conte went on to note that Patreon isn't making the cuts because it wants to replace employees with AI. "To be clear about the impact of AI on today's decision: we are not making the above changes because we believe AI replaces humans," he wrote. "The more we have learned to use these new tools, the clearer it has become that they are not substitutes for the creativity, judgment, detail orientation, or craftsmanship that our teammates have in spades, nor do they replace the desire for human connection that all of us cherish so deeply. That's my personal opinion, but more importantly, it's the foundation of Patreon's strategy: our product vision and business are both predicated on the value of human creativity and human connection." He continued, "AI has fundamentally transformed the tech industry, though, including how we work, how we build products, how we communicate, and more. That does have an impact on how we operate and organize." Beyond the headcount reduction, Conte said Patreon is also restructuring how it operates, "flattening" its organizational chart and refocusing teams around its top priorities. Affected employees will receive at least 16 weeks of severance pay, plus an additional week for every year worked, healthcare coverage through the end of the year, and a $1,500 stipend to replace their company laptop. Last week, Patreon announced that it was partnering with internet infrastructure provider Cloudflare to directly block access to AI bots designed to train their AI models on creators' work without permission. The company said it had to enhance its efforts on this front because AI scraping has become more sophisticated. The move came as online publishers and creators are grappling with AI companies using their work to train AI models. Patreon's latest round of layoffs is the platform's largest since it cut 17% of its staff back in 2022. During that earlier round of layoffs, Patreon also closed its offices in Berlin and Dublin.

title: Alexa Plus is getting an AI update to handle more complicated instructions
teaser: Alexa Plus is getting a major AI upgrade, letting it manage complex tasks—like finding the right washing machine cycle—by connecting to dozens of smart home brands.
summary:
Amazon is upgrading Alexa Plus with new AI capabilities, allowing it to handle complex, multi-step instructions. The update connects Alexa to a wider range of smart home devices (including brands like Bosch, Delta, and iRobot), enabling advanced functions such as selecting correct washing machine cycles based on instructions.

These improvements are bolstered by the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open-source standard. MCP allows AI models to interface with external systems, paving the way for integrations from companies like Canva, Headspace, and Priceline. For instance, Priceline will soon enable users to book hotels and trips directly via Alexa Plus.
author: Emma Roth
content: Amazon is launching an update to its Alexa Plus assistant that will allow it to connect to smart home devices in new ways. With the update , which is currently in preview, Alexa Plus can link up with tech from Bosch, Delta, Ecovacs, iRobot, Yale Home, Whirlpool, Tapo, Eufy, and others, while automatically routing requests to the correct device. In an example shared by Amazon, a person with a supported washing machine can say, "Alexa, my kid's soccer jersey could use a deep clean, but the tag says cold wash only." From there, Alexa Plus would navigate the washer's cycle options and choose the correct setting. The new integrations are powered by Amazon's new AI developer toolkit, which is supposed to make it easier for device makers to connect to Alexa Plus, "including those with unique capabilities that weren't supported before." Amazon widely launched its revamped AI assistant in February , which can handle multi-step requests and help you create routines using your voice. It currently only performs tasks in a limited number of third-party services, such as Ticketmaster, OpenTable, Uber, Thumbtack, Expedia, Yelp, Square, and Angi . But Amazon is trying to change this by adopting the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open-source standard that allows AI models to connect to external systems and tools. This will give more brands the ability to interact with Alexa Plus, with Canva, Headspace, Priceline, Lyft, Cengage, Virgin Atlantic, Weekend, and other companies launching integrations later this year. For example, Priceline will give customers the ability to browse hotel options and book a trip directly through Alexa Plus. Priceline, along with Atom Tickets, Cengage, Fandango, and Taskrabbit, will soon support payments through Amazon Wallet as well.

title: Technology — Ratepayer bill gains steam
teaser: A bipartisan bill aims to stop tech companies from passing power costs to consumers, passing the House with a 52-0 vote.
summary: The bipartisan Ratepayer Protection Act aims to shift the financial burden of electricity infrastructure from individual consumers to large technology companies. The legislation, which passed the House Energy and Commerce Committee in a strong 52-0 vote, mandates that state regulators hold hearings to consider standards requiring data centers to pay for the costs of new power or lines. However, the bill does not force the adoption of these standards, merely the consideration. Supporters argue this will prevent price spikes caused by data center expansion. The effort gained momentum with the introduction of a companion bill in the Senate by Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio), bolstering its chances of becoming law.
author: The Hill
content: The bipartisan Ratepayer Protection Ac t would require states to "consider" standards that put the costs on tech companies, rather than individuals. Its supporters say it could help alleviate potential price spikes caused by power-hungry data centers, but critics say it doesn't go far enough to solve the problem. The legislation advanced out of the House Energy and Commerce Committee on Tuesday in a 52-0 vote , a strong display of bipartisan support and a reflection of how the backlash to the data center buildout has crossed party lines. The measure, which aims to codify a White House pledge signed by tech giants earlier this year, forces state regulators to hold a hearing on a standard that would ensure that large data centers pay for the cost of new power or power lines stemming from their electricity use. It does not force them to actually adopt such standards. "[I]t has become clear that across the entire industry there is one entity uniquely positioned to stand up for families and communities who are the ones paying electricity bills-and that is this Committee, and our colleagues in Congress," House Energy and Commerce Chair Brett Guthrie (R-Ky.) said in a statement. The Ratepayer Protection Act also recently got a companion in the Senate, bolstering its chances of becoming law. Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) introduced the measure in the upper chamber last week. A spokesperson for the senator said in a statement that he is "encouraged by the bipartisan support and committee passage in the House" and will continue working with the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee to get the bill "across the finish line in the Senate." Read more in a full report at TheHill.com .

title: AegisAI banks $36M as AI spear-phishing surges fivefold in a year
teaser: AI-spear phishing attacks surged fivefold. AegisAI is raising $36M with AI agents to stop threats manipulating human trust.
summary: Email security startup AegisAI Inc. raised $36 million to combat the rapid rise of sophisticated, AI-generated spear-phishing attacks. AegisAI developed a defense using autonomous AI agents that analyze the 'intent and identity' behind messages, rather than just looking for patterns. The company notes that AI spear-phishing has surged fivefold in a year, rising from 2.8% to 13.9% of observed malicious emails. According to AegisAI co-founder Cy Khormaee, the greatest risk is no longer technical, but psychological: the threat is 'AI model manipulating someone in your organization.' The new funding allows AegisAI to scale its defense, which was pioneered by former Google security experts.
author: Duncan Riley
content: Email security startup AegisAI Inc. today said it has raised $36 million in new funding to counter a fast-growing class of artificial intelligence-generated email attacks that no amount of employee training can reliably stop. The San Francisco company builds its own large language models to guard corporate inboxes. The pitch rests on how much the phishing lure has changed. An attacker used to need time and skill. Now AI does the legwork. It scrapes the web for details about the target. It works out which colleague or vendor that person leans on. Then it drafts a note in that trusted voice, at scale. AegisAI calls the technique AI spear-phishing, and it says the capability now runs about the price of a cup of coffee. The company runs a network of autonomous AI agents inside the inbox. Traditional filters look for patterns lifted from past scams. AegisAI's agents read the intent and identity behind each message, an approach it says catches linguistically flawless attacks that clear every technical check. The company claims it cuts false positives by up to 90% against legacy tools. AI-generated spear-phishing made up 2.8% of the phishing AegisAI observed in early 2025 and reached 13.9% by the end of the year. That finding comes from a study the company presented at this year's M3AAWG conference, drawn from a pool of more than 20,000 malicious emails. The AI notes were also harder to stop. They reached the inbox at close to twice the rate of human-written attacks. Of the ones that got through, almost 73% had cleared email authentication, sent from real accounts that attackers had quietly taken over. The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation's latest Internet Crime Report lands in the same place. Victims reported a record $20.8 billion in losses last year. Business email compromise, which turns on identity rather than malware, made up $11.64 billion of that. Ransomware and malicious software combined did not come close. "The most immediate, catastrophic risk to your organization isn't an AI agent hacking your firewall. It's an AI model manipulating someone in your organization into handing over the keys," said Cy Khormaee, co-founder and chief executive of AegisAI. "You cannot patch human trust. When the attack is AI, the defense has to be AI." Khormaee started the company in 2025 with Ryan Luo. The two spent years in Google LLC's core security group, where they helped build reCAPTCHA, Safe Browsing and Web Risk. AegisAI launched publicly in September and has since signed dozens of customers across fintech and technology, including crypto payments company Mesh Connect Inc. and AI developer platform LangChain Inc. At web privacy company firm Lokker, it says its agents caught an attack routed through a vendor's compromised Salesforce Inc. systems, a message that carried no malicious link or attachment. The new money will scale AegisAI's roster of defense agents and push toward general availability for Vanguard, the company's threat-hunting agent that works outside the inbox. Introduced in March, Vanguard follows suspicious links and attachments onto the open web and returns a threat report within minutes Battery Ventures LP led the Series A round, with existing backers Accel Partners LP and Foundation Capital joining. Dharmesh Thakker, a general partner at Battery Ventures, said generative AI "just broke every assumption legacy email security was built on," leaving a machine-speed defense as the only viable answer. The financing brings AegisAI's total raised to $49 million, less than a year after its public launch. title: Mobileye CEO Amnon Shashua to step aside as company pushes into robotaxis, robotics
teaser: Mobileye founder Amnon Shashua steps down just as the company accelerates into the future of self-driving, planning robotaxis and humanoid robots.
summary: Mobileye founder and CEO Amnon Shashua plans to step down after nearly three decades, coinciding with the company's major pivot into advanced robotics and autonomous driving. Mobileye, which began with computer vision chips derived from Shashua's Hebrew University research, was previously acquired by Intel for $15.3 billion in 2017 and spun back publicly in 2022. The company's next phase, dubbed 'Mobileye 3.0,' focuses heavily on robotics and automotive AI. To support this push, Mobileye recently acquired Shashua’s humanoid robotics startup, Mentee Robotics, for $900 million. Furthermore, the company has committed to expanding beyond its supplier role by launching its own robotaxi service in a U.S. city by 2027.
author: Kirsten Korosec
content: Mobileye founder and CEO Amnon Shashua plans to step down from the top leadership post after nearly three decades, just as the company pushes into robotaxis and humanoid robots. Shashua will remain CEO until Mobileye hires a replacement, according to a regulatory filing Thursday. Mobileye got its start making computer vision chips based on Shashua's academic research at Hebrew University in Israel, and grew into a major supplier of the chips that power automotive safety and driver-assistance features. It had the largest IPO in Israel's history, was acquired in 2017 by Intel for $15.3 billion, then spun back out as a publicly traded company in 2022, though Intel remains its largest shareholder. Under Shashua, Mobileye also moved beyond selling chips to automakers and began building its own systems that handle autonomous driving , which it now supplies to Volkswagen and its MOIA subsidiary. In January, the company acquired Shashua's humanoid robotics startup Mentee Robotics for $900 million , which Shashua called part of "Mobileye 3.0," the next phase of the business focused on robotics and automotive AI. Mobileye also said in June it would expand beyond its supplier status to launch its own robotaxi service in a U.S. city in 2027.

title: MeBeMe’s new ‘interrupter’ app helps you become your best self instead of doomscrolling
teaser: The MeBeMe app turns phone distractions into positive habits, giving users real-world 'missions' instead of endless scrolling.
summary: MeBeMe is a new "interrupter" app designed to combat doomscrolling by encouraging users to build positive habits rather than restricting phone use. Instead of blocking distracting apps, MeBeMe guides users toward self-improvement through personalized 'missions' or tasks. Users select an identity—such as 'lifelong learner' or 'athlete'—and the app sends occasional prompts (e.g., watching an educational video or attending a book club) aligned with that role. The app offers over 75 identities and emphasizes user privacy, requiring no account and storing data locally. Developed by Eric Wolfram, it is currently free for iOS and developing for Android.
author: Lauren Forristal
content: MeBeMe is a new app that acts as an "interrupter," designed to help users become their best selves instead of getting lost in endless scrolling. Rather than blocking access to their phones, the app delivers small "missions" or tasks that encourage real-world habits aligned with the person users want to become. The app joins a growing wave of anti-doomscrolling tools as more people look for ways to reduce social media addiction. What sets MeBeMe apart is its approach: instead of locking users out of distracting apps, it nudges them toward meaningful actions. To get started, users choose an identity they want to embody, such as a "lifelong learner." MeBeMe then sends occasional notifications with quick tasks related to that identity. For example, it might suggest watching an educational video for seven minutes. Someone who selects the "classics reader" identity could receive a mission to attend a local book club or lecture. The app offers more than 75 identities across several categories. Under "Mind," users can choose roles like mathematician, scientist, historian, or chess player. The "Body" category includes athlete, dancer, cyclist, and runner. There are also categories focused on relationships and home-based interests like cooking and gardening. Users can select multiple identities at once, allowing them to build habits across different areas of their lives. Image Credits: MeBeMe Users also control how often they receive notifications, whether that's daily or just occasionally. A feature called "Break Your Scroll" even uses Siri to read the messages aloud. MeBeMe officially launched last Wednesday. It was created by Eric Wolfram , who originally built the app for his son before realizing it was just as helpful for himself. "Small actions, repeated over time, shape who you are," Wolfram writes on his website. "Becoming who you are is a lifelong project." Wolfram also says privacy is one of MeBeMe's defining features. The app requires no account, stores all user data on the device, and allows users to turn off anonymous usage data sharing. MeBeMe is available as a free download for iOS devices, with an Android version coming soon. There are no ads or subscriptions.

title: Geekbench 7 will push your computer or phone even harder for better benchmarking
teaser: Geekbench 7 is here: The updated benchmark uses new video/audio tests (AV1, Opus) and redesigned multi-core tests for more accurate hardware stress testing.
summary: Primate Labs has launched Geekbench 7, the latest version of its benchmarking tool, designed to stress test computers and phones with greater accuracy. Key upgrades include new, comprehensive video and audio encoding/decoding tests that incorporate codecs like AV1 and Opus, and a redesigned multi-core test that better reflects real-world software behavior. The tool also utilizes larger, more demanding datasets for CPUs and GPUs. While the benchmarks still run quickly, the new tests aim to capture the true hardware demands of modern applications. Note that Geekbench 7 Pro licenses are $99 (discounted to $79 until August 6th), and crucially, all scores from Geekbench 6 are incompatible with the new version.
author: Antonio G. Di Benedetto
content: Primate Labs is releasing Geekbench 7 , the latest generation of its popular benchmarking tool. Geekbench 7 features new video and audio encoding / decoding tests, a redesigned multi-core test, and larger, more demanding datasets for CPUs and GPUs to crunch through. It otherwise looks and acts just like Geekbench 6, and a Pro license will cost the same $99 (discounted to $79 until August 6th). A Geekbench 7 Pro license allows for offline benchmarking that doesn't get uploaded to the Geekbench Browser , and it still covers all compatible desktop platforms of Windows, macOS, and Linux. Geekbench is one of the mainstay synthetic benchmarks we use in reviewing laptops here at The Verge . I've always liked how simple and fast Geekbench is to run, but its short duration also means it's a better test of quick bursts of computing rather than sustained loads that can throttle some CPUs and GPUs. (One of its tests involves rendering a 1.5MB PDF file, which must be near-instantaneous for most modern chips.) Primate Labs claims Geekbench 7 uses "more demanding data sets to more accurately capture the hardware demands of modern applications." The new audio / video tests also now include AV1, Opus, model video conferencing, streaming, and content consumption workloads. And multi-core benchmarks are designed to better reflect real software behavior since the new workloads will only run multi-threaded when the modeled tasks run that way. These all sound like marked improvements, even if Geekbench 7 tests still only take a few minutes to run. Scores from Geekbench 6 are of course not compatible with Geekbench 7. So if you're the testing type, feel free to spiritually join me in a whole bunch of new benchmark testing and retesting. Always be testing.

title: Lego’s Donkey Kong arcade machine lets Mario jump endless barrels — Miyamoto is reportedly happy
teaser: The LEGO Donkey Kong machine features a complex 'barrel pump' that creates an infinite barrel loop using a stack of 14 barrels.
summary: This article details the elaborate mechanical engineering of a LEGO arcade machine based on Donkey Kong. The centerpiece is the 'barrel pump,' which operates using a stack of 14 barrels and a capacity of 20. This system creates an impressive 'infinite barrel loop' as barrels roll slowly from top to bottom and are continuously recycled. Designing this was a major challenge, solved by combining LEGO elements like studs, slopes, and Technic beams to mimic natural rolling motion. Character movement is handled by a complex dual system: the joystick uses a long lever connected to a dingler for horizontal movement, while the jump button operates via a seesaw lever, simulating jumping using gravity.
author: Sean Hollister
content: Q: How does the barrel mechanism work, and how many barrels fit inside of it at a time? The barrel mechanism is essentially a pump. It uses a stack of 14 Barrels going up the side of the model. Each time the barrel lever is pulled, it adds one barrel to the bottom of the stack and one falls out the top. The system holds 20 barrels so there can be 6 barrels rolling down at a time. Q: Do the barrels roll all the way down to the bottom? Do they fall out of the set, and need to be reinserted into the slot, or does the mechanism bring them back to the top? The barrels roll all the way from the top to the bottom where they are collected in a hopper that is connected to the barrel pump. This forms an infinite barrel loop which is, by definition, "barrels of fun". Q: What was the biggest hurdle in designing and testing that mechanism? The biggest challenge was getting the barrels to roll down slowly without stopping or getting stuck. This was achieved through a combination of rolling over steps, LEGO studs, slopes, bows and using LEGO Technic beams which are slightly thinner than LEGO Bricks. This allowed us to capture the feeling of the gameplay where the barrel rolls down slowly. I rolled thousands of barrels down those tracks to figure it out... Those barrels drove me bananas! The second biggest hurdle was finding a way to get the barrel from the bottom to the top again. We built all kinds of stuff; things to shoot one barrel from the bottom to the top, worm gears, force multiplication levers, and more. But it turned the right answer was simply a lot more barrels. Q: How do the joystick and button make Jumpman/Mario move? The joystick moves Jumpman from left to right using a long lever up the back of the model, connected to a dingler. The jump button uses a similar mechanism used in a piano key. When it is pressed down in front of the model, the other end of a see-saw lever presses up on a long rod with Jumpman at the top. When the button is released gravity returns Jumpman to the bottom.
